newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish ex-PM Haughey to testify on mystery cash.
newsitem.headline: Irish ex-PM Haughey to testify on mystery cash.

text.p: Former Irish Prime Minister Charles Haughey, bon-viveur, kingmaker and accountant, is expected to tell an official tribunal this week how he forgot about the million pounds he was given by a chain store tycoon.

Haughey is set to testify at a payments-to-politicians tribunal investigating why Ben Dunne, whose family owns Ireland's premier department store chain, gave vast sums in a scandal that has forced one government minister to resign.

The ex-premier's appearance will climax a drama that has kept the nation on the edge of its seat since newspapers reported last year that a mysterious former member of the powerful Fianna Fail party had received 1.3 million Irish pounds ($2 million).

Last week Haughey, issued a statement through his legal team admitting for the first time that he was the recipient of the cash, reversing a string of denials. He also admitted misleading his lawyers.

The statement said that legal papers submitted to the tribunal had jogged his memory and Haughey, who has not appeared before the tribunal, is expected to take the stand some time this week, probably on Tuesday, according to its officials.

The affair has caught the public imagination because of its revelations about links between Ireland's rich and powerful, and raised calls for investigations into links between politics and business and new laws to govern party fund-raising.

Haughey's star part has also rekindled interest in how a chartered accountant whose career earnings from politics totalled little more than half a million pounds came to own a mansion, stud farm, a private island and enjoy a jet-set lifestyle.

The affair claimed its first political scalp last year when former Transport Minister Michael Lowry resigned after acknowledging media reports that Dunne had paid for the quarter-million pound renovations and extension of his private family home.
The tribunal began its work when a coalition of Fine Gael, led by then-prime minister John Bruton, the Labour party and Democratic Left were in power and Fianna Fail in opposition.
But Fianna Fail, led by Prime Minister Bertie Ahern, came to power after June 6 elections and is facing opposition calls for another tribunal to be set up to investigate Haughey alone.

Ahern said last week that the current tribunal would have to run its course but said he was keeping an "open mind" about any new investigation into one of the most powerful political figures in Irish politics since self-rule seven decades ago.

Haughey was prime minister three times between 1979 and 1992. His friends included the late French President Francois Mitterrand. His tastes, chronicled in Ireland's tabloid press, were lavish and included fine art, fine wine and fine clothes.

All major political parties have testified that they received funds from Dunne for campaigning and other purposes. There has been no suggestion that political favours were either asked for or received by anyone.
The affair came to light in a feud within the the Dunne family, whose green-fronted department stores are a familiar sight in every Irish town.

Dunne was dropped from the family business five years ago in a scandal over his arrest by Florida police in the company of a call girl and a quantity of cocaine. He was acquitted of drug trafficking and went for substance abuse treatment.
Members of the Dunne family have since been at loggerheads over a joint trust fund and what was paid out of it.

Dunne said he gave Haughey the money because the former prime minister was in financial difficulties. The money was channelled through Des Traynor, a partner in an accountants' firm with Haughey who has since died.
